title: Brute Force Login Response
overview: Repeated failed authentication against SSH, RDP, VPN, web portals or cloud accounts, including password spraying (many users, few passwords) and credential stuffing. Key question: did the attacker only guess the password (password compromise, blocked by MFA) or get in (account compromise)?
indicators: Spike of failed logins from one IP, or one account hit from many IPs
Many usernames tried with the same few passwords (spray)
Success right after a long run of failures
Low-and-slow attempts under the lockout threshold with very regular timing
Source IP is a Tor exit node or has a bad reputation; legacy authentication in use

severity_guidance.critical: A login succeeded from the attacking IP, or a privileged/admin/server account was accessed
severity_guidance.high: High-volume attack on an internet-facing system, no confirmed success yet
severity_guidance.medium: Moderate failures against a standard account from an external IP
severity_guidance.low: A few failures from an internal IP that look like mistyped passwords

false_positive_checks: Source is an internal workstation and the user then logged in normally or reset their password
Source is an approved scanner or monitoring system
A service account with an expired password is retrying automatically

steps.action: Count failed attempts, the time window and the accounts targeted.
Check the source IP reputation (Tor, known attacker, internal vs external).
Determine whether a successful login followed the failures from the same IP or for the same account.
Identify the pattern: one IP many accounts (spray), many IPs one account, or low-and-slow regular timing.
If a login succeeded, review the account's activity afterwards: new device or location, new processes, privilege changes, data access.
Check whether MFA is enabled and whether the attacker had the password but failed MFA.
Decide true or false positive and set severity using the severity guidance.
Recommend containment (needs approval) and create a ticket with the evidence.

containment_recommendations: Block the attacking IP at the firewall (attackers rotate IPs, so monitor for new ones)
If compromise is suspected: disable the account, reset the password and revoke active sessions
Enforce MFA, rate limiting and lockout; block legacy authentication
escalation_criteria: Any login succeeded after the failures
A privileged, admin or server account is involved
Suspicious activity continues after the IP is blocked
Signs of data access or exfiltration

title: Phishing Email Response
overview: Emails that impersonate a trusted sender to steal credentials or deliver malware. Workflow: confirm the message, scope who received it, check who interacted, look for follow-on activity, then contain.
indicators: Lookalike sender domain, or SPF/DKIM/DMARC failure
Urgent wording; link text that differs from the real URL
Risky attachment types (.html, .iso, macro-enabled Office files)
Same message sent to many recipients, or campaign variants

severity_guidance.critical: Credentials entered by a privileged or finance user and a suspicious sign-in followed
severity_guidance.high: User clicked the link or opened the attachment
severity_guidance.medium: Delivered to many users but no interaction found
severity_guidance.low: Blocked at the gateway, or a known benign sender or internal simulation

false_positive_checks: SPF, DKIM and DMARC all pass and the sender is a known vendor
Message headers show an internal phishing simulation
The domain is on the approved sender list

steps.action: Review the reported email, headers and attachments; extract the Message-ID, sender and URLs.
Check the sender domain and URLs for suspicious indicators.
Find all recipients and whether the message was delivered, blocked or quarantined.
For each recipient, determine whether they opened it, clicked a link, opened the attachment or entered credentials.
If credentials may be exposed, look for new or unusual sign-ins after the click.
If an attachment was opened, check the endpoint for malware execution.
Decide true or false positive and set severity using the severity guidance.
Recommend containment (needs approval) and create a ticket.

containment_recommendations: Remove the message from all mailboxes
Block confirmed malicious senders, domains and URLs (only when the evidence supports it)
Isolate a suspicious attachment or the affected endpoint
If credentials were entered: reset the password and revoke sessions; review mailbox rules and forwarding
escalation_criteria: Credentials were submitted
A privileged or finance user is involved
Phishing is confirmed and widespread (many recipients)
A suspicious sign-in or malware execution follows the click

title: Malware Detection Response
overview: AV/EDR alerts about malicious executables, droppers, trojans and ransomware. Ransomware needs the fastest response: stop the spread, preserve evidence, restore from clean backups. Ransomware can also hide an earlier, unresolved compromise.
indicators: File hash flagged malicious on threat intelligence
Office app or browser spawning PowerShell, cmd or script hosts
Mass file renaming, new extensions or a ransom note
Backup or shadow-copy deletion; security tools disabled
Connections to a known command-and-control destination

severity_guidance.critical: Ransomware activity, or malware on a server or domain controller
severity_guidance.high: Known-malicious file executed on a workstation or contacting C2
severity_guidance.low: Adware/PUA, or an admin tool flagged by EDR with an approved ticket

false_positive_checks: Flagged file is a legitimate admin tool used by IT under an approved change ticket
AV action shows quarantined and executed=false
The hash is on the approved software list

steps.action: Review the detection details: affected device, user, file path and AV/EDR action (blocked or allowed).
Collect the file hash and any contacted IP or domain, and check them against threat intelligence.
Find the parent process and execution time on the endpoint.
Check whether the same hash or behaviour appears on other hosts.
Look for ransomware signs: mass file changes, backup deletion, ransom note.
Decide true or false positive and set severity using the severity guidance.
Recommend isolating the device if compromise is suspected, and request analysis by the security team before any evidence is deleted.
Create a ticket with the hash, host and timeline.

containment_recommendations: Isolate the affected host from the network (powering off loses evidence in memory; use only if it cannot be disconnected)
Do not delete the file or wipe the machine until the security team has captured evidence
Reset credentials used on the host; contain other systems that could give the attacker access
Do not recommend paying a ransom
escalation_criteria: Any ransomware behaviour
A server or domain controller is affected
The same malware appears on more than one host
Signs of data theft or C2 communication

title: Suspicious Network Traffic Response
overview: Firewall, IDS or DNS alerts about C2 beaconing, DNS tunnelling, port scans and unusual outbound transfers. Attackers hide C2 inside common protocols (HTTP/S, DNS, mail); inside a network, SMB, SSH and RDP can carry traffic between pivot hosts.
indicators: A common protocol used by an abnormal process, with high outbound bytes or irregular ports
Fixed-interval connections to a rare destination (beaconing)
Long, high-entropy DNS queries (possible tunnelling)
Large off-hours transfer to an unknown external IP
One host probing many ports or many hosts

severity_guidance.critical: Confirmed C2 or exfiltration from a server holding sensitive data
severity_guidance.high: Beaconing from a workstation, or a large unexplained outbound transfer
severity_guidance.medium: External port scan against the perimeter with no sessions established
severity_guidance.low: Known scanner, or a scheduled job such as a nightly backup

false_positive_checks: Source is an approved vulnerability scanner inside its scan window
Traffic matches a scheduled backup or sync job
Destination is on the approved vendor or cloud allowlist

steps.action: Review the destination, protocol, ports and volume of the traffic.
Check the destination IP or domain reputation.
Compare with normal behaviour for that asset's role (what protocols and destinations are usual?).
Search firewall, proxy and endpoint logs for related events: timing, frequency, the process and user behind it.
Check whether the traffic matches an approved job or scanner schedule (false positive).
Decide true or false positive and set severity using the severity guidance.
Recommend blocking only when the malicious activity is sufficiently supported by evidence.
Create a ticket with the destination, volume and timeline.

containment_recommendations: Block the destination at the firewall and DNS, only with sufficient supporting evidence
Isolate the source host if C2 or exfiltration is confirmed
Apply protocol-based egress filtering and IDS/IPS signatures for known malware traffic
escalation_criteria: Suspected or confirmed data exfiltration
Beaconing to a known-bad destination
Ongoing compromise indicators on the source host
Sensitive data or a server is involved

title: Privilege Escalation Response
overview: An account or process gains higher rights than intended: abuse of UAC or sudo, a vulnerability exploit, an unapproved admin-group change, or a new admin account. The deciding question is whether a valid, approved change ticket explains it.
indicators: Windows: UAC-bypass registry changes, unusual parent-child processes, unsigned elevated processes
Linux: real and effective user ID differ, setuid/setgid changes, privileged binaries run by unprivileged users
Standard user added to Administrators, sudoers or Domain Admins
New local admin account created outside a change window
Known exploit tooling or a vulnerable service spawning a root/SYSTEM shell

severity_guidance.critical: Unauthorised user obtains Domain Admin or root
severity_guidance.high: Unapproved admin/sudo change on a server, or exploit tooling executed
severity_guidance.medium: Change with a ticket that is still pending approval
severity_guidance.low: Change matching an approved change ticket

false_positive_checks: An approved change ticket matches the user, host and time
An on-call emergency access is documented
The actor is an authorised IT admin acting inside a maintenance window

steps.action: Identify who made the change, on which host, from which IP, and when.
Check the change-management ticket: approved, pending or none.
Review the account's activity after the change.
Review sudo/audit logs, process trees and registry or group-membership changes around the event.
Check the source IP and the host for known vulnerable software (CVE/CVSS).
Decide true or false positive and set severity using the severity guidance.
Recommend revoking the elevated rights if the change is unauthorised (needs approval).
Create a ticket with the change, the actor and the evidence.

containment_recommendations: Revoke the elevated rights and disable the account if the change is unauthorised
Patch the vulnerable software; rotate credentials of affected privileged accounts
Prevention: highest UAC level, sudo timestamp_timeout 0 with tty_tickets, manual approval for just-in-time elevation
escalation_criteria: Any unauthorised admin or root access
A domain-level privilege change
Exploit tooling executed on a server
No matching change ticket and no plausible explanation
references: MITRE ATT&CK T1548.003 Sudo and Sudo Caching: https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1548/003/

title: General Alert Triage
overview: Fallback when the alert type is unclear. Follows the standard incident lifecycle (detect, analyse, contain, eradicate and recover, review) and the SOC flow: classify, investigate, escalate or close.
indicators: Alert does not match any specific alert type
Mixed or ambiguous indicators

severity_guidance.critical: Active compromise, data loss or ransomware; respond immediately
severity_guidance.high: Likely true positive with significant impact; respond within 1 hour
severity_guidance.medium: Suspicious, needs investigation; respond the same day
severity_guidance.low: Likely benign or informational; review in batch

false_positive_checks: Source belongs to an approved scanner, backup job or administrator
A change ticket or maintenance window explains the activity
The same alert fired before and was closed as benign

steps.action: Extract indicators: IPs, domains, file hashes, usernames.
Check each indicator against threat intelligence.
Pull related authentication, firewall, web and endpoint logs around the alert time.
Map the behaviour to a MITRE ATT&CK technique and re-classify into a specific alert type if possible.
Decide true or false positive and set severity using the severity guidance.
Escalate or close, and create a ticket recording the decision.

containment_recommendations: Choose containment based on the re-classified alert type
escalation_criteria: Severity is high or critical
Evidence shows a successful compromise
The alert cannot be explained after investigation
references: CISA, Incident and Vulnerability Response Playbooks: https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/news/incident-and-vulnerability-response-playbooks
